title: JSON File Persistence
subtitle: Using JSON files as a simple data store — read, update, and atomic write patterns
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Small tools, prototypes, and scripts need a simple way to persist data without setting up a database. JSON files provide human-readable, structured persistence with no dependencies.
whyItExists.solution: Read with fs.readFile + JSON.parse, modify in memory, write back with fs.writeFile + JSON.stringify. For safety, write to a temp file first, then rename (atomic swap) so a crash never corrupts the original.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Config files, small data stores (< a few thousand records), CLI tool state, test fixtures, prototypes. When you outgrow JSON files, migrate to SQLite (better-sqlite3) or a proper database.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use JSON files for concurrent writes from multiple processes (race condition — last writer wins). Don't use them for large datasets or queries that need indexing — use SQLite or a database.

explainModes.beginner: Reading a JSON file: read the file as a string, then JSON.parse() it to get a JavaScript object. Writing: JSON.stringify() converts your object to a string, then write it to the file. This is how config files, package.json, and simple data files work in Node.js.
explainModes.simple: Read: const data = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('data.json', 'utf8')). Write: await fs.writeFile('data.json', JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)). Atomic write: write to temp → fs.rename to final path (rename is atomic on most OSes). Create-if-missing: try { read } catch { return default }. Update record: read → modify array → write back. Always stringify with null, 2 for readable formatting.
explainModes.standard: JSON.stringify(data, null, 2): the 2-space indent makes files readable and produces clean diffs. JSON.parse reviver: second argument to parse — transform values during parsing (e.g., date strings to Date objects). JSON.stringify replacer: second argument to stringify — exclude fields or transform them. Concurrent write problem: if two requests write simultaneously, one may overwrite the other. Solutions: an in-memory store with periodic flush, or a proper database. For local tools, accept the limitation.
explainModes.technical: Atomic write (POSIX): write to a temp file in the same directory, then fs.rename(tempPath, finalPath). POSIX rename is atomic within the same filesystem — the final path either has the old content or the new content, never a partial write. On Windows, rename is not guaranteed atomic. node-atomically package handles cross-platform atomicity. BSON (MongoDB's binary JSON): faster parse/stringify, supports more types (Buffer, Date, ObjectId). Used internally by MongoDB drivers. JSON5 / TOML: superset formats with comments, trailing commas — use for config files where developer-friendliness matters.
explainModes.deepDive: Large JSON files: reading with readFileSync loads the whole file into memory. For files > 100MB, use streaming JSON parsers (JSONStream, stream-json) that emit objects as they're parsed. JSON5/JSONC: the json5 package parses JSON with comments and trailing commas. tsconfig.json uses JSONC. Zod for config validation: z.object({}) validates the parsed JSON against a schema at load time — fail early with a clear error if the file has wrong structure. Lock files (lockfile-js, proper-lockfile): prevent concurrent writes by requiring a lock before reading/writing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of writing to a temp file first and then using fs.rename() when saving JSON data?
options: It makes the write faster by using disk cache
POSIX rename is atomic — if the process crashes during the write, the original file is untouched. Without it, a crash mid-write leaves a corrupted file.
It prevents other processes from reading the file while writing
It compresses the JSON data automatically
questions.explanation: fs.writeFile writes directly to the target path — if the process crashes halfway through (power loss, OOM kill), the file can be left partially written and corrupt. Writing to a .tmp file first means the target always has either the old content (rename not yet called) or the new content (rename completed). POSIX rename is atomic at the filesystem level — it's a single directory entry update, not a data copy.

faq.q: When should I switch from JSON files to a real database?
faq.a: Switch when: (1) you have concurrent writers (multiple requests at the same time) — JSON files have race conditions. (2) Your data grows past a few thousand records — no indexing, full scan on every read. (3) You need queries, filtering, or joins. SQLite (via better-sqlite3 or Bun's built-in) is a great step up — file-based like JSON but with full SQL, transactions, and indexes. Add PostgreSQL or MySQL when you need multi-server access.
